sources.title: AI That Works: No Vibes Allowed: Performance Engineering
sources.note: meta.md only, no transcript; description only, no ideas carded.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: things that agents are good at are things with back pressure
cards.claim: Agents do well where the loop gives automatic, deterministic feedback (compile, run, inspect), and badly where the outcome is not machine-checkable.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrated with a Ralph-Wiggum compiler build loop (spec, write program, compile, run); no numbers.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md or ship plan: prefer phases whose success is checkable by a script; flag phases lacking a check

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's not good at assessing visual things
cards.claim: Screenshot-based self-checking is weak backpressure for UI because model vision cannot get things pixel perfect, even with a browser feedback loop.
cards.evidence_detail: His own motion-graphics attempt the day before: overlaps and gaps in lines the agent could not fix.
cards.landing: Web manager UI phases: do not accept agent screenshot review as a verifier; require owner look or measured signal

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: basically doing a taste approximation it can go and pull the data
cards.claim: Replace agent taste judgement with production metrics: ship several variants behind flags and let the agent read conversion data as its own backpressure.
cards.evidence_detail: Hypothetical conversion rates of 3%, 7%, 5% across three variants; no real experiment.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (single-tenant shop app, little traffic); maybe ops console metrics

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: turn it on at 0.01%, make sure nothing's broken
cards.claim: Agents may merge to production but a gradual ramp (tiny percentage, then widening over hours or days) with an agent reviewing metrics at each step should switch features on.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as the 'real magic' in discussion; no case study.
cards.landing: Deploy path (manual railway up, mobile EAS builds): staged rollout of mobile builds; settings-gated features already like dispatcher default OFF

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: two dimensions of how you activate your feature flags
cards.claim: A flag can be activated along population (percentage or cohort) and along duration, and what matters is what you do with the outputs of that activation.
cards.evidence_detail: Whiteboard discussion, endorsing Vaibhav's framing.
cards.landing: shop_setting registry / enable_dispatcher gating: time-boxed enablement as a pattern

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: they spend a lot of their time running around cleaning up feature flags
cards.claim: Staff engineers at large teams spend much time cleaning stale flags; abandoned experiments leave dead code paths and lost context, so every flag needs an owner and an exit.
cards.evidence_detail: From HumanLayer's work with staff engineers on teams of hundreds or thousands; no counts.
cards.landing: Ship plan: any default-OFF flag (dispatcher, advances) gets a removal/decision date in the decisions journal

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: take twice as long and you go clean up the parts of the code base
cards.claim: Pay down mess incrementally by cleaning the code you touch on each feature (Ron Jeffries style) instead of scheduling big refactors.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites a Ron Jeffries refactoring post; Vaibhav says his team does this plus occasional rewrites.
cards.landing: Phase routine: a 'leave touched code cleaner' line; or nowhere obvious

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every deployment in a large distributed system is an experiment
cards.claim: Every deploy is a rollout, so schema and API changes must support old and new versions side by side (new table or endpoint, old path kept).
cards.evidence_detail: Prompted by a viewer question on DB schema changes behind flags; SaaS has two live versions vs shipped software with many.
cards.landing: Alembic migration rules in CLAUDE.md (NOT VALID then VALIDATE, deploy ordering); mobile APKs in the field already create a multi-version fleet

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't try to do that from day one because you're going to spend three months
cards.claim: Build backpressure automation incrementally: start with a CLI or MCP that queries the metrics and a manual agent session, automate the loop only later, to avoid building a software factory before learning.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience-based failure case he says he sees ('people try to over automate this on day one'); no numbers.
cards.landing: Ship plan sequencing: manual-first before saving workflows or building verifier pipelines

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Short and sweet
cards.claim: The deploy/PR-to-production gap is the bottleneck of agent-speed shipping; manual review after the PR is the slow stage, which a prod-data experiment step in CI could shorten.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex restates Vaibhav's whiteboard (write/test loop is hot, PR to deploy is slow); Dex endorses it in the outro.
cards.landing: CI: a job running checks on prod-shaped data; phase routine's reviewer step

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we're only allowed to have like 10 live experiments at a time
cards.claim: Cap the number of concurrently live experiments Kanban-style so new ones must displace old ones (Vaibhav's proposal, Dex frames it as a work-in-progress limit).
cards.evidence_detail: Framing of Vaibhav's idea of reserving a traffic slice for experiments; speculative runtime semantics.
cards.landing: WIP limit on open draft PRs or live default-OFF features; nowhere obvious

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: your engineering time is usually a lot worth a lot more than the tokens
cards.claim: Use the smartest model until token cost exceeds engineering cost, then do the engineering to cut spend (week of work to move to a cheaper model).
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as advice the show gives repeatedly; no figures.
cards.landing: Verifier effort routing: default high effort until measured cost justifies tuning
cards.inventory_ref: ### June 2026 (#60 Agents that Work in Any Language)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every time someone complains I just take the complaint and paste it
cards.claim: Turn every complaint into a new eval and iterate the prompt until all tests pass, creating internal backpressure.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes his own practice on HumanLayer's cloud inference ('the very expensive GEPA').
cards.landing: Register ids with fail-before/pass-after: a complaint becomes a test; knowledge-store diagnoses
cards.inventory_ref: ### June 2026 (#60 Agents that Work in Any Language)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's just breaking down a five hundred line function into smaller functions that are testable
cards.claim: Narrow edge steps (translate in, translate out) are easy to eval because their input range is small, like decomposing a big function into testable pieces; the core pipeline's evals are untouched.
cards.evidence_detail: Remark during the pipeline design; backtest in the demo shows English-only answers without the pipeline (no numbers given).
cards.landing: Narrow single-purpose agents/workflows with their own checks, rather than one large prompt
cards.inventory_ref: ### June 2026 (#60 Agents that Work in Any Language)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: what you name the fields tells the model what they should be
cards.claim: Output schema field names are part of the prompt and can leak steering; competing instructions lean on instruction following and lower the success rate.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside during live demo; no measurement.
cards.landing: Naming of fields in register/journal templates and skill frontmatter; nowhere obvious
cards.inventory_ref: ### June 2026 (#60 Agents that Work in Any Language)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The difference between software that's right 99 percent of the time and 99.999
cards.claim: A small drop in instruction-following (95% to 92%) matters because the gap between 99% and 99.99% accuracy is the gap between trusted and constantly broken software; heavy system prompt steering narrows outcomes.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's paraphrase on the show (transcript wording: 'ninety nine percent ... ninety nine point nine nine percent'); hypothetical percentages.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md length/adherence argument: per-rule compliance compounds across hundreds of lines
cards.inventory_ref: ### June 2026 (#60 Agents that Work in Any Language)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you kind of like accumulate your own like little collection of mini bench
cards.claim: Keep a private text file of git SHAs plus prompts that recreate problems which cost you a week, as a personal benchmark for any new model.
cards.evidence_detail: His own practice; example is an old HumanLayer race condition (Claude Code approvals correlated to the wrong session).
cards.landing: P1 cold-resume trial style fixtures: frozen SHA plus prompt as a repeatable harness test; model-upgrade regression set

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable still fails our at least it can't one shot
cards.claim: Fable 5 given a three-sentence symptom prompt at the pre-fix SHA added correlation but keyed it on a non-unique identifier, missing the root cause (use the upstream tool call ID).
cards.evidence_detail: One run on one benchmark; correct answer is mapping the unique tool-call ID into the database.
cards.landing: Verifier choice: stronger model did not remove the need for human-held answer keys

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: one shot problem is like less of a useful evaluation of the gap in quality
cards.claim: A one-shot attempt is a poor test of model quality; test a goal or Ralph-style loop that runs for hours, since a slow model that finds what no human found still matters.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites the model finding a ten-year-old FFmpeg vulnerability as an example; not his experiment.
cards.landing: Model/effort routing evaluation method: judge by loop outcomes and cost, not single-shot answers

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you don't own the code and the architecture, you are signing yourself up
cards.claim: Without owning the code and architecture you will eventually face a bug no model can untangle across many moving pieces and have to spend a week re-onboarding by hand.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributes the framing to Jake Nations; HumanLayer lost a week around October 2025 on a daemon/socket/MCP/API race.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial and knowledge store: keep human-readable architecture facts the owner can recover from

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you've just like doubled your effectiveness basically
cards.claim: A model that cuts the corrections needed per conversation from five to two roughly doubles effectiveness, so small constraint-holding gains justify switching.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers (5 to 2 corrections), not measured.
cards.landing: Model routing: measure corrections per phase as the comparison metric

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Codex is very robotic. It's clearly not meant for a human to use.
cards.claim: Design docs, plans and research written by Codex read as robotic and unfit for human readers, whereas Claude output reads more like nice sentences.
cards.evidence_detail: Impressions during the live session; no comparison data.
cards.landing: Owner one-page view and reviewer output: readability for the human as a selection criterion
